SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY AND QUARTERLY
  INVESTMENT ACTIVITY REPORTS FOR DECEMBER 2025

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Receive and file the December 2025 monthly and quarterly investment activity
  reports for the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency.

BACKGROUND

Pursuant to Section 16 of the City and Successor Agency Investment Policy, the City
Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on investments to
the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The reports shall
detail the type of investment, issuer’s name, purchase date, maturity date, amount of
deposit, and interest rate. This information shall be provided for all City and Successor
Agency pooled investments and for Certificates of Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax
Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts, and Community Facilities District accounts
managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly and quarterly investment reports provide a synopsis of the City and
Successor Agency’s investment activity. They provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations. The interest rates
presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly and Quarterly Investment Reports December 2025
February 3, 2026
Page 2

DISCUSSION

Compliance with Investment Policy

For December, the City’s invested portfolio totaled $304,112,309, an increase of
$9,337,049 from the previous month and $8,332,493 decrease from prior year. The
monthly increase was due to a transfer of excess funds from property taxes from
General Fund to the Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF).

As of December, the par value of the Successor Agency’s portfolio was $8,935,771.
This represents a decrease of $340,672 from the previous month, resulting from the
required transfer of ROPS funds to the General Fund for ERAF and SERAF obligations.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, US Treasury Securities, and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies: 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and,
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to meet the
City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the City invests in two
pooled funds, the Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and the California Asset
Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily operational activities and
can be used during economic uncertainties for ongoing operating and maintenance
needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio, ensuring the City and Successor
Agency meet their cash flow requirements.

The City’s LAIF balance at the end of December was $115,815,128, an increase of
$12,000,000 due to the transfer of funds from the General Fund to LAIF.

The Successor Agency’s LAIF balance at the end of December was $3,985,613, no
changes from the prior month.

The City’s CAMP balance at the end of December was $54,090,7455 compared to
$53,910,080 in November. The increase is due to interest earned.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly and Quarterly Investment Reports December 2025
February 3, 2026
Page 3

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of December 31, 2025, the interest rates for LAIF and CAMP investments
were 4.025 percent and 3.95 percent, respectively. By comparison, the LAIF and CAMP
interest rates at the end of November were 4.096 percent and 4.10 percent. This time
last year, LAIF and CAMP rates were at 4.434 percent and 4.73, respectively.

The chart above shows the LAIF and CAMP average monthly yields from March 2025
through December 2025. The difference between the two funds’ performance is
primarily due to their varying pool characteristics. CAMP’s portfolio composition is more
prone to market volatility, resulting in performance variations.

Diversity

The Finance Division aims to diversify investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks associated with specific security types or individual
financial institutions.

The City and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly diversified. The
monthly and quarterly reports include all investments held by both entities and current
book values as of December 31, 2025.

The City and Successor Agency are expected to have sufficient funds to meet their
expenditure requirements for the next six months. The Finance Division will continue to
monitor current economic conditions and the impact on interest rates.

Attached are summaries of the investments in the City and Successor Agency’s books
as of December 31, 2025.

 Key Terms and Definitions

  Term  Definition
 Adjustment Frequency  For adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), the number of months between the loan’s or security’s coupon adjustment dates. GNMA ARMs adjust annually in one of the following months: January, April, July, or
  October; FNMA and FHLMC issues also usually have annual reset dates although the adjustment dates occur at any time during the year.
 Book Yield  Usually provided from Bond Accounting reports and represents the Annualized yield to maturity (or call) based on the book value of a bond and projected cash flows. Similar to “Projected Yield at Book”
  except 3mo Historical Speeds are commonly employed in calculating Book Yield for amortizing securities rather than a forward looking estimate.
 Collateral  Assets that are used to secure payment of certain bonds, for example, real estate is a source of collateral for mortgage backed securities.
 Coupon  The stated interest rate on a bond that is used to calculate interest payments that are payable to bond holders. A coupon rate of interest can be fixed over the life of the bond or a variable rate of interest that is
  calculated using a formula described in the offering documents. Floating coupon rates are generally a simple spread (or margin) relative to a stated index (such as LIBOR). Many bonds include caps and floors
  on the coupon interest rate and some contain more complex formulas.
 Convexity  An incremental measure (along with the linear measure of duration) to capture the curvature of a bond’s price/yield relationship. Practically, negative convexity indicates the upside price of a bond is limited if
  rates fall due to embedded options (mortgage prepayments or an issuers ability to call the bond).
 Current Face (Par Amount)  Computed by multiplying the original face by the current factor, represents principal remaining for an investor to receive.
 Current Index  The level of the index at a specified moment in time that is used in conjunction with the margin to establish the security’s coupon.
 Effective Duration  Or “option-adjusted duration” measures interest rate risk of a security considering the impact of optionality and possible changes in future interest rates. It is calculated by averaging the percentage changes
  in the security's value under the higher and lower rate environments, while 25bp, 50bp or other sized yield shifts are commonly used, the rate of change is restated as a 100bp equivalent by simple
  multiplication.
 Enhanced Credit Rating  A rating that reflects the underlying issue’s standalone credit quality as well as any credit support provided by a state credit enhancement program.
 Factor  Relevant for bonds that pay amortizing principal to bond holders. The factor equals the percentage of the original face that is outstanding.
 Floor  For adjustable-rate securities, it is the lowest level to which a coupon can fall over the life of the security
 Forward Curve  The forward curve is a graph that defines the prices (yields) at which a contract for future delivery or payment can be concluded today, it represents a term structure of forward rates.
 Gross WAC  The weighted-average mortgage rate of all the loans in a pool.
 Initial Reset Date  The date on which an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) or underlying mortgage in an ARM pool can reset for the first time.
 Internal Rate of Return  A sector or portfolio yield to expected maturity based on the portfolio's expected cash flows, treated as a single instrument. The reflects the overall yield to expected maturity of the portfolio, not a monthly
  earnings rate. On a single bond, IRR is the same as yield.
 Lifetime Cap  For adjustable-rate securities, it is the highest level that a coupon may attain over the life of the security.
 Margin  The amount added to the index of a floating rate loan or security (such as an adjustment rate mortgage security) in order to calculate a coupon rate of interest.
 Market Yield  The yield of a bond at current market price. For a bond you own, an indication of what yield the market will pay you today for the bond.
 Months to Roll (MTR)  Months remaining until a bond’s coupon will next reset
 Pay Window  For CMO’s, the expected date range to receive principal payments.
 Prepay Speeds  Prepayments occur when a servicer receives principal payments above the scheduled amount. The velocity of the prepayments is measured using prepayment speeds, typically measured using conditional
  prepayment rate (CPR) or prepayment speed assumption (PSA).
 Price Volatility  The percentage change in price for a given a change in interest rates. Price volatility is generally calculated using a parallel, instantaneous shock in a benchmark yield curve assuming constant spreads
  relative to the benchmark curve.
 Projected Call  The date at which a callable bond is projected to be redeemed at a given level of interest rates. All things equal, higher rates should extend the date and lower rates should accelerate the redemption date.
 Projected Yield at Book  Annualized yield to maturity (or call) based on the book value of a bond and projected cash flows given the market conditions at the time of the analysis.
 Roll Date  The date (or weighted average date) that a bond’s coupon can reset
 Static Cash Flow Gap Estimate  In the absence of more robust Earnings at Risk simulations, an estimate of how sensitive a depository’s margin is to movements in interest rates by comparing the amount and sensitivity of repricing Assets
  and Liabilities. A positive gap indicates more assets repricing than liabilities (asset sensitive) and a negative gap indicates more liabilities repricing than assets (liability sensitive).
 Tranche  Class of debt securities issued as part of a bond instrument, each part (tranche) characterized by a unique set of features such as maturity, interest (coupon) rate, interest payment date, to suit the needs of
  different investors.
 Underlying Credit Rating  A rating issued by an agency assessing the ability of an issuer to repay its debt. The assessment of creditworthiness is based solely on the obligor and does not include enhancements from a third party.
 Weighted Average Life (WAL)  The weighted-average time in years that the principal of a security is expected to be outstanding. For mortgage securities and callable bonds, average life varies with prepayment speeds and yield curve
  assumptions.
 Weighted Average Loan Age (WALA)  The average age of all mortgages in a pool, weighted by current balance.
 Weighted Average Maturity (WAM)  The average remaining maturity of the underlying mortgages in a pool, weighted by current balance.
 Yield at Book Price  On a sector or portfolio summary level, this is a book value-weighted average yield. It reflects expected earnings in the current month. Over time, relatively low (or high) yields may mature, increasing (or
  decreasing) subsequent months' expected earnings versus the initial weighted average.
 Yield Contribution  For a given a sectors weight, how much yield does it contribute to the overall portfolio.

 Yield to Maturity (YTM)  The single yield that makes the present value of the cash flows to maturity equal to the price plus accrued interest.

 Yield to Worst (YTW)  The lower of the yield to maturity and the yield to call.

 Key Terms and Definitions

  Term  Definition
 Adjustment Frequency  For adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), the number of months between the loan’s or security’s coupon adjustment dates. GNMA ARMs adjust annually in one of the following months: January, April, July, or
  October; FNMA and FHLMC issues also usually have annual reset dates although the adjustment dates occur at any time during the year.
 Book Yield  Usually provided from Bond Accounting reports and represents the Annualized yield to maturity (or call) based on the book value of a bond and projected cash flows. Similar to “Projected Yield at Book”
  except 3mo Historical Speeds are commonly employed in calculating Book Yield for amortizing securities rather than a forward looking estimate.
 Collateral  Assets that are used to secure payment of certain bonds, for example, real estate is a source of collateral for mortgage backed securities.
 Coupon  The stated interest rate on a bond that is used to calculate interest payments that are payable to bond holders. A coupon rate of interest can be fixed over the life of the bond or a variable rate of interest that is
  calculated using a formula described in the offering documents. Floating coupon rates are generally a simple spread (or margin) relative to a stated index (such as LIBOR). Many bonds include caps and floors
  on the coupon interest rate and some contain more complex formulas.
 Convexity  An incremental measure (along with the linear measure of duration) to capture the curvature of a bond’s price/yield relationship. Practically, negative convexity indicates the upside price of a bond is limited if
  rates fall due to embedded options (mortgage prepayments or an issuers ability to call the bond).
 Current Face (Par Amount)  Computed by multiplying the original face by the current factor, represents principal remaining for an investor to receive.
 Current Index  The level of the index at a specified moment in time that is used in conjunction with the margin to establish the security’s coupon.
 Effective Duration  Or “option-adjusted duration” measures interest rate risk of a security considering the impact of optionality and possible changes in future interest rates. It is calculated by averaging the percentage changes
  in the security's value under the higher and lower rate environments, while 25bp, 50bp or other sized yield shifts are commonly used, the rate of change is restated as a 100bp equivalent by simple
  multiplication.
 Enhanced Credit Rating  A rating that reflects the underlying issue’s standalone credit quality as well as any credit support provided by a state credit enhancement program.
 Factor  Relevant for bonds that pay amortizing principal to bond holders. The factor equals the percentage of the original face that is outstanding.
 Floor  For adjustable-rate securities, it is the lowest level to which a coupon can fall over the life of the security
 Forward Curve  The forward curve is a graph that defines the prices (yields) at which a contract for future delivery or payment can be concluded today, it represents a term structure of forward rates.
 Gross WAC  The weighted-average mortgage rate of all the loans in a pool.
 Initial Reset Date  The date on which an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) or underlying mortgage in an ARM pool can reset for the first time.
 Internal Rate of Return  A sector or portfolio yield to expected maturity based on the portfolio's expected cash flows, treated as a single instrument. The reflects the overall yield to expected maturity of the portfolio, not a monthly
  earnings rate. On a single bond, IRR is the same as yield.
 Lifetime Cap  For adjustable-rate securities, it is the highest level that a coupon may attain over the life of the security.
 Margin  The amount added to the index of a floating rate loan or security (such as an adjustment rate mortgage security) in order to calculate a coupon rate of interest.
 Market Yield  The yield of a bond at current market price. For a bond you own, an indication of what yield the market will pay you today for the bond.
 Months to Roll (MTR)  Months remaining until a bond’s coupon will next reset
 Pay Window  For CMO’s, the expected date range to receive principal payments.
 Prepay Speeds  Prepayments occur when a servicer receives principal payments above the scheduled amount. The velocity of the prepayments is measured using prepayment speeds, typically measured using conditional
  prepayment rate (CPR) or prepayment speed assumption (PSA).
 Price Volatility  The percentage change in price for a given a change in interest rates. Price volatility is generally calculated using a parallel, instantaneous shock in a benchmark yield curve assuming constant spreads
  relative to the benchmark curve.
 Projected Call  The date at which a callable bond is projected to be redeemed at a given level of interest rates. All things equal, higher rates should extend the date and lower rates should accelerate the redemption date.
 Projected Yield at Book  Annualized yield to maturity (or call) based on the book value of a bond and projected cash flows given the market conditions at the time of the analysis.
 Roll Date  The date (or weighted average date) that a bond’s coupon can reset
 Static Cash Flow Gap Estimate  In the absence of more robust Earnings at Risk simulations, an estimate of how sensitive a depository’s margin is to movements in interest rates by comparing the amount and sensitivity of repricing Assets
  and Liabilities. A positive gap indicates more assets repricing than liabilities (asset sensitive) and a negative gap indicates more liabilities repricing than assets (liability sensitive).
 Tranche  Class of debt securities issued as part of a bond instrument, each part (tranche) characterized by a unique set of features such as maturity, interest (coupon) rate, interest payment date, to suit the needs of
  different investors.
 Underlying Credit Rating  A rating issued by an agency assessing the ability of an issuer to repay its debt. The assessment of creditworthiness is based solely on the obligor and does not include enhancements from a third party.
 Weighted Average Life (WAL)  The weighted-average time in years that the principal of a security is expected to be outstanding. For mortgage securities and callable bonds, average life varies with prepayment speeds and yield curve
  assumptions.
 Weighted Average Loan Age (WALA)  The average age of all mortgages in a pool, weighted by current balance.
 Weighted Average Maturity (WAM)  The average remaining maturity of the underlying mortgages in a pool, weighted by current balance.
 Yield at Book Price  On a sector or portfolio summary level, this is a book value-weighted average yield. It reflects expected earnings in the current month. Over time, relatively low (or high) yields may mature, increasing (or
  decreasing) subsequent months' expected earnings versus the initial weighted average.
 Yield Contribution  For a given a sectors weight, how much yield does it contribute to the overall portfolio.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2026-004, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale, dissolving the Palmdale Civic Authority.

BACKGROUND

The Palmdale Civic Authority (PCA) was established in 1976 as a Joint Powers Authority
(JPA) between the City of Palmdale and the Community Redevelopment Agency of the
City of Palmdale pursuant to a Joint Powers Agreement. The purpose of the PCA was
to support civic and redevelopment-related activities consistent with the objectives of
the former redevelopment agency.

The governing structure of the PCA is set forth in its Amended and Restated Bylaws,
which provide that the Authority is governed by a five-member Board of Directors
consisting of the members of the Palmdale City Council. The Bylaws further establish
the Authority’s officers, meeting requirements, and operational framework, and
expressly contemplate the dissolution of the Authority under specified conditions.

In 2012, the Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale was dissolved
pursuant to State law, and the City of Palmdale became the successor agency,
assuming responsibility for the former agency’s assets and obligations. Since that time,
the Authority has had no active operational role. According to City records, the entity
currently has no outstanding indebtedness, no assets, no liabilities, no ongoing
activities, and is not a party to any material contracts.

Article IV, Section 3 of the Amended and Restated Bylaws authorizes dissolution of the
Authority with the approval of all Members, provided that at the time of dissolution the
Authority has no outstanding indebtedness and is not a party to any outstanding material
contracts. Upon dissolution, any remaining assets, after payment or provision for
payment of liabilities, are to be distributed to the Members of the Authority.

Government Code section 6510 further authorizes the termination of a JPA upon
completion of its purposes or when it is no longer necessary.

DISCUSSION

The proposed Resolution would formally dissolve the Palmdale Civic Authority,
consistent with the requirements of the Joint Powers Agreement, the PCA Bylaws, and
applicable provisions of the California Government Code. As documented in the
Resolution, the Authority no longer serves an operational purpose, as the Community
Redevelopment Agency, one of its founding members, has been dissolved, and the City
of Palmdale now serves as the successor agency.

Staff has confirmed that the PCA has no outstanding debts, liabilities, assets, or
contractual obligations. Accordingly, the conditions required for dissolution under Article
IV, Section 3 of the Amended and Restated Bylaws have been satisfied. Because there
are no assets or liabilities to distribute, dissolution will not result in any fiscal or
operational impacts to the City.

Adoption of the Resolution will allow the City to formally conclude the Authority's
existence, eliminate an inactive governmental entity, and ensure that City records
accurately reflect the current organizational structure. The action does not affect any
obligations or assets of the City in its role as successor agency and pertains solely to
the formal dissolution of the Palmdale Civic Authority.

$0; There is no fiscal impact associated with the recommended action.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9642 with Maestro Development, LLC, Construction
  Management and Observation Services for PN 851, Melville J. Courson Park
  Revitalization Project (Project), for a total not to exceed amount of $456,500, which
  includes a contract amount of $415,000, plus a 10% contingency amount of
  $41,500, for a term of 360 working days from the date of the Notice to Proceed;

  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-
  9642 with Maestro Development, LLC, including minimal and/or non-substantial
  changes; and,

  3. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to approve contract
  amendments for additional or changed scope of work up to the 10% contingency
  amount approved by the Council.

BACKGROUND

Melville J. Courson Park is located at the corner of 10th Street East and East Avenue Q-
12. On May 4, 2022, the Council approved the design phase of the Project for renovations
to include:

    Restroom facility, drinking fountain, storage building, and Pet Waste Station;
    Playground for 5 to12 year olds;
    Challenge course, exercise stations, and fitness zones;

    Raised bandstand/stage, plaza paving, and concrete decomposed granite paths;
    Picnic areas, park furnishings, and shade pavilion;
    Therapeutic and meditation garden, security fencing and lighting;
    Flagpole, Monument sign, and trash enclosures; and,
    New irrigation, shade trees, and drought-tolerant landscaping.

The Project has successfully transitioned from the design phase and is now entering the
construction phase. Construction Management and Observation Services are needed to
oversee the project through construction. In general, construction management and
observation services shall provide the following scope of services, including, but not
limited to:

    Constructability Review: Conducting a final technical evaluation of the design
  plans to ensure project feasibility before the work begins.

    Construction Management and Observation: Managing all phases of construction
  projects from initial mobilization through final closeout to ensure compliance with
  plans and specifications and to maintain the construction schedule and stay
  within the project budget.

DISCUSSION

The City publicly advertised for construction management and observation services for
the Melville J. Courson Park Revitalization Project via PlanetBids on August 28, 2025.
While 22 vendors registered as potential consultants, the solicitation closed on October
20, 2025, with nine (9) bidders submitting formal proposals:

Following a comprehensive evaluation including reference checks and interviews, staff
recommend that the City Council award the contract for Project No. 851 (Construction
Management and Observation services) to Maestro Development, LLC, in the amount
of $415,000, plus a 10% contingency amount of $41,500.

BACKGROUND

The Anaverde Creek Watershed includes approximately 10,065 acres in the
southwestern region of Palmdale. Runoff flows from southwest to northeast, gathering
runoff from the Sierra Pelona mountains and lower alluvial plain areas, and ultimately
collecting in Anaverde Creek. Peak elevations in the watershed are greater than 5,180
feet, while the outlet of Anaverde Creek at Highway 14 has an elevation of approximately
2,760 feet. Flooding has historically been observed downstream of the creek’s outlet at
Highway 14, as evidenced by the area being mapped by Federal Emergency

outcome of this contract, the City wishes to develop and implement a strategy to mitigate
the floodplain, thereby opening this area to future development.

DISCUSSION

On September 26, 2025, a Request for Qualifications was advertised electronically
through PlanetBids to solicit Statements of Qualifications (SOQ) for professional
services to update the Anaverde Creek Watershed Master Drainage Plan and the design
of drainage basins near Avenue R and Division Street.

On October 27, 2025, the proposal deadline, three (3) Statements of Qualifications were
received. These SOQ were evaluated based on five criteria by three reviewers. Each
reviewer scored the SOQ independently:

 Vendor  Location  Fees
 1. Pacific Advanced Civil Engineering, Inc.  Fountain Valley, CA  $1,311,869
 2. CWE  Fullerton, CA  $1,157,582
 3. Craftwater Engineering, Inc.  Pasadena, CA  $2,321,383

All firms were invited for an interview and tendered the fee proposals. Based on the
interviews, qualifications, favorable reference checks, and extensive experience in
providing the City with flood protection design services, the staff recommends PACE for
the award of the professional services contract for a proposed fee of $1,311,569.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Hold a public hearing to accept public testimony; and,

  2. Receive and file the Fiscal Year (FY) 2025-26 Annual Employee Vacancy Report,
  in accordance with Assembly Bill 2561.

BACKGROUND

On September 22, 2024, Governor Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2561 (AB 2561) into
law, which became effective on January 1, 2025. AB 2561 requires public agencies to
address the status of vacancies. The California Legislature recognized that vacancies
in the public sector pose challenges that can and negatively impact the delivery of public
services.

DISCUSSION

AB 2561 requires the City to present the status of vacancies, recruitment efforts, and
retention efforts at a public hearing held at least once each fiscal year prior to adoption of
the annual budget. Specifically, the statute requires public agencies to:

    Report job vacancies, recruitment, and retention efforts;
    Identify policies or practices that may lead to obstacles or negatively impact the
  hiring process;
    Provide recognized bargaining units an opportunity to participate in the public
  hearing; and,

SUBJECT:  LEGISLATIVE AND LITIGATION UPDATE REGARDING FEDERAL
  IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Receive and file legislative and litigation update regarding federal immigration
  enforcement.

BACKGROUND

On July 11, 2025, the federal court issued a preliminary injunction against federal
enforcement agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),
prohibiting the detention of individuals based on one, or a combination of the following
factors: 1. Race/ethnicity; 2. Speaking Spanish or speaking English with an accent; 3.
Presence at a particular location (e.g. bus stop, car wash, tow yard, day laborer pick up
site, agricultural site, etc.); and, 4. The type of work one does.

In response to this ruling, the LASD amended its operational processes to include specific
procedures to identify federal agents by on-scene LASD officers, including direction to
request identification or agency credentials and record the encounter on the officer’s
body-worn camera.1 On or about July 29, 2025, Los Angeles County intervened in the
federal suit.

On August 1, 2025, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the lower court’s ruling. On
September 8, 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court granted a stay of the district court’s July 11
injunction, pausing that injunction nationwide while appeals proceed. A more limited
injunction on access to counsel procedures at B-18, a detention facility in Los Angeles,
remains in place — but it applies only to that specific detention facility and that specific
constitutional claim.

1 July 11, 2025, LASD Newsletter.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Legislative and Litigation Update Regarding Federal Immigration Enforcement
February 3, 2026
Page 2

On December 9, 2025, Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors adopted an ordinance
prohibiting law enforcement officers from wearing facial coverings that obscure their face
and personal disguises and requiring law enforcement officers to wear visible
identification when performing duties that involve interaction with the public. The
ordinance provides for exceptions to these requirements for undercover, protective, and
Special Weapons and Tactics operations and exigent circumstances. The ordinance
applies to incorporated areas of Los Angeles County.

The State enacted SB 805 No Vigilantes Act and SB 627 No Secret Police Act, which
took effect on January 1, 2026. SB 805 revises California’s impersonation laws to
explicitly cover federal law enforcement officers and imposes misdemeanor penalties.2 It
requires any law enforcement agency operating in California, including federal law
enforcement, to maintain and publicly post a written policy on the visible identification of
sworn personnel.3 Any law enforcement officer operating in California that is not
uniformed must visibly display identification that includes their agency and either a name
or badge number to the public when performing their enforcement duties, except as
specified.4 A violation of these provisions is a misdemeanor.

SB 627 prohibits a law enforcement officer, including federal law enforcement, from
wearing a facial covering that conceals or obscures their facial identity in the performance
of their duties, except as expressly authorized.5 Law enforcement agencies operating in
California must also maintain and publicly post a written policy regarding the use of facial
coverings.6

LASD is in the process of crafting their policies required by SB 805 and SB 62 but have
provided notice of the prohibition against wearing facial coverings to its officers.7 The
state’s authority to enforce the new laws, SB 805 and SB 627, against the federal
government is currently being challenged in federal court.8

The Department of Homeland Security has publicly declared that it will not comply. The
case is pending and LASD awaits judicial guidance prior to proceeding with those
provisions of law applicable to federal law enforcement.

DISCUSSION

The City contracts LASD for police services. There have been no changes to LASD’s
operational policy from July 11, 2025.

LASD’s revised operational process responds and addresses concerns related to ICE
officer identification, enforcement policy, and third-party impersonators. LASD’s
procedures follow the California Values Act (SB 54), which prohibit LASD from assisting
with federal civil immigration enforcement. LASD officers may act in response to federal
immigration enforcement operations to maintain public order, ensure the safety of
community members, and protect the lives and safety of federal law enforcement
officers involved in the operation, including the enforcement of state criminal laws.

While local law enforcement is prohibited from assisting with immigration enforcement
pursuant to State law, pursuant to department operational process, LASD officers will
attempt to identify, document, and record ICE agents and activities when responding
on-site in accordance with department policy. This process addresses complaints
related to ICE enforcement, the identification of ICE agents, and third-party
impersonators.

Beginning January 1, 2026, all law enforcement agencies operating in California are
prohibited from wearing facial coverings that conceal or obscure their facial identity while
performing their duties, except as expressly authorized. All law enforcement officers not
in uniform must visibly display identification that includes their agency and either a name
or badge number to the public when performing their enforcement duties. The
application of these requirements to the federal government awaits adjudication. LASD
will update and post their policies regarding masks and officer identification as required
by state law.

  ENCOUNTERS INVOLVING POSSIBLE

  PURPOSE

  This Newsletter provides guidance to Department personnel when responding to reports or encounters
  involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or other federal agencies conducting immigration
  enforcement activities within the County. These operations often raise public concern and require a response
  from Department personnel that prioritizes safety, policy compliance, and public trust.

  BACKGROUND

  The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department may receive calls for service involving suspected immigration
  enforcement activity, including incidents where federal agents may be operating in the community, near
  schools, businesses, or homes. These incidents can cause public confusion, fear, and unrest, especially
  when the agents are in unmarked vehicles, unidentifiable, or decline to show identification to community
  members.

  In these instances, California Senate Bill 54, or the California Values Act which enacted and amended
  Government Code sections 7282 through 7282.5, and added sections 7284 through 7284.12 and County
  policy generally prohibit Department personnel from participating in civil immigration enforcement.
  Department personnel must remain neutral, avoid direct involvement in immigration enforcement, and ensure
  their actions are consistent with Department policy, the law, and the safety of the community.

  DEPUTIES

  When encountering or being dispatched to a situation possibly involving immigration enforcement, deputies
  should:

  Immediately notify a field supervisor, if a supervisor is not already assigned to the incident, of a

  Attempt to identify the federal agents. If the individuals are acting in an enforcement capacity but are not
  clearly identifiable, deputies should:

  Request identification or agency credentials from the on-scene federal supervisor or agent-in-
  charge. If there is no on-scene supervisor or agent-in-charge, request identification or agency
  credentials from the individuals acting in an enforcement capacity.

  Record the encounter on body-worn camera, including identification efforts.

  If the individuals decline to identify themselves, observe from a safe distance and document (such
  as in a log, incident report, and/or body worn camera):

  Physical descriptions of individuals

  Agency markings (if any)

  Number of personnel involved

  Vehicle descriptions and license plates

  If it is determined that an incident involves federal immigration enforcement conducted by federal agents, the
  actions of Department members should be limited to those authorized under California law. Department
  personnel may act to maintain public order, ensure the safety of community members, and protect the lives
  and safety of federal law enforcement officers involved in the operation. This may include enforcing California
  criminal laws, when necessary, particularly those related to public safety and public order, such as acts of
  violence, unlawful assembly, or vandalism.

  Deputies should focus on crowd control and public safety, ensuring the situation does not escalate into
  violence;

  Remain neutral. Deputies should use de-escalation techniques to prevent conflicts between ICE agents
  and the public;

  Deputies should avoid physical involvement or assistance in the immigration arrest/enforcement action
  while maintaining neutrality unless the situation presents a clear and present officer-safety situation for
  the federal agents;

  The incident should be thoroughly documented, including any actions taken by deputies and federal
  agents, in an MDC log entry or an incident report if necessary. Deputies should also notify a field
  supervisor immediately;

  Deputies should clearly communicate to members of the public that the Department is not involved in
  immigration enforcement and is present to ensure public safety; and

  25-11 - Face Covering/ Identification of Law Enforcement Personnel

  VOLUME 25 NUMBER 11  DATE: December 17, 2025

  FACE COVERING/ IDENTIFICATION OF
  LAW ENFORCEMENT PERSONNEL

  PURPOSE

  This informational newsletter is designed to inform Department members about California Senate Bill 627,
  codified in California Penal Code section 185.5, that bans law enforcement officers from wearing facial
  coverings that conceal or obscure their facial identity (including ski masks, gaiters, and similar opaque face
  coverings) in the performance of their duties.

  This law goes into effect on January 1, 2026.

  Department personnel must ensure compliance with the law which prohibits wearing facial coverings, unless
  covered by the statutory exceptions.

  BACKGROUND

  California Penal Code section 185.5, enacted by California Senate Bill 627, prohibits federal and local law
  enforcement officers from wearing facial coverings as defined (including, but not limited to, ski masks,
  balaclavas and neck gaiters) during law enforcement operations. This law provides for exceptions to the
  facial covering prohibition, including for undercover law enforcement operations, officers performing Special
  Weapons and Tactics responsibilities, and medical needs.

  Please note that the provisions as applied to federal law enforcement officials is under review by judicial
  authorities. The Department will wait for judicial guidance before proceeding with that provision of the law.

  In addition, California Government Code section 7289 was added, which requires that by July 1, 2026, law
  enforcement agencies operating in California maintain and publicly post a written policy regarding the use of
  facial coverings, with specified requirements, including a list of narrowly tailored exemptions. The Department
  is in the process of crafting that policy.

  To support the enactment of these laws, the legislature made several findings including that “the routine use of
  facial coverings by law enforcement officers has significant implications for public perception, officer-
  community interactions, and accountability.”

  PROVISIONS OF SB 627:

  Defines Face Coverings: Defines "facial covering" for purposes of newly added Penal Code section
  185.5 as any opaque mask, garment, helmet, headgear, or other item that conceals or obscures the
  facial identity of an individual, including, but not limited to, a baclava, tactical mask, gator, ski mask, and
  any similar type of facial covering or face-shielding item.

  The law specifies that "facial covering" does not include:

  a translucent face shield or clear mask that does not conceal the wearer's facial identity and is
  used in compliance with the agency's policy and procedures;

  a N95 medical mask or surgical mask to protect against transmission of disease or infection;

  air-purifying respirators, or self-contained breathing apparatuses necessary to protect against
  exposure to toxin, gas, smoke, inclement weather or any other hazardous or harmful environmental
  conditions,

  a mask or device necessary for underwater use;

  a motorcycle helmet when worn by an officer using a motorcycle or other vehicle that requires a
  helmet for safe operations; or

  eyewear necessary to protect from the use of retinal weapons.

  Bans Face Coverings: Prohibits the wearing of masks (such as neck gaiters, ski masks) while in the
  performance of law enforcement operations.

  Specifies Exceptions: Allows face coverings for Special Enforcement Bureau (Special Weapons and
  Tactics - SWAT) in the performance of SWAT responsibilities, active undercover operations or
  assignments, tactical operations where protective gear is required for physical safety, the protection of
  identity during prosecution, and as may be required by law for occupational health and safety and/or a
  reasonable accommodation.

  Agency Policies: Mandates that agencies create policies to comply with the law by July 1, 2026.
  Allows a member of the public, an oversight body, or a local governing authority to submit a written
  challenge to the legality of these policies. Provides that agencies have 90 days to correct any
  deficiencies and permits complaining parties to seek judicial review of challenged policies.

  Criminal Penalties: Imposes criminal penalties for willful and knowing violations of the prohibition and
  provides that the specified criminal penalties will not apply to any law enforcement officer if they were
  acting in their capacity as an employee of the agency and the agency maintains and publicly
  posts a written policy pursuant to Government Code section 7289.

  Civil Penalties: Imposes civil penalties for officers who commit tortious conduct while violating the
  facial covering prohibition including assault, battery, false imprisonment, false arrest, abuse of process
  or malicious prosecution.

  In addition to the state law, Los Angeles County is advancing its own ordinance to prohibit law enforcement
  from masking. Effective January 8, 2026, the County ordinance prohibits the wearing of masks or disguises
  while interacting with the public when working in unincorporated areas of Los Angeles County.

  If you require further information, contact Field Operations Support Services at (323) 890-5411 or
  fossunit@lasd.org.
